item.title: Cache Proxies for Ephemeral CI Runners
item.description:
ephemerd gives every CI job a brand new runner. A new container on Linux, a new VM on macOS and Windows. The job runs, the runner is thrown away, and the next job starts from a clean image. That is the whole point. Nothing a job does can leak into the next one.

Clean has a cost. A fresh runner has an empty cache. So every job downloads the world again. Go modules, crates, the Rust toolchain, Composer packages, release tarballs. On a busy repo that is gigabytes a day, pulled over and over, most of it byte-for-byte identical to what the last job pulled.

item.title: Ephemeral macOS Runners: A Fresh VM Per Job on Apple Silicon
item.description:
ephemerd gives every CI job a brand new environment and throws it away after. On Linux and Windows that environment is a container. On macOS it can’t be. Apple’s license wants macOS running on Apple hardware, so the Mac in my rack is the real thing. The isolation comes from a VM instead.

Each macOS job gets a fresh Virtualization.framework VM cloned from a base image. The job runs inside it. The VM is destroyed when the job finishes. That’s the same contract as the container path. Getting there took four fixes that I only found by running the fleet. This post walks the VM lifecycle and the three ways it bit me:

item.title: ePHPm Odds and Ends: OOM-Killed Links, Opcode Scanning, WebSockets and a 44 ms Stall
item.description:
Not every fix in ePHPm earns a full write-up. A few of the smaller ones have stuck with me because the lesson in each was bigger than the diff. Here are four from this summer.

A release build the OOM killer kept eating

ePHPm statically links libphp, ICU and a pile of other C libraries into one Rust binary. It ships for four targets. For the v0.4.2 performance release I set the release profile to lto = "fat" with codegen-units = 1 (#171). Fat LTO pulls every crate’s LLVM IR into one module in one process and optimizes it as a unit. One codegen unit removes the parallelism that would otherwise spread that memory out. That’s one very large process at the final link.

item.title: shipmates Short Ones: 8 Minutes Extracting Go, and Three Voice-Loop Bugs
item.description:
A few shipmates bugs don’t need a whole post each. They were too good to leave in commit messages, though.

setup-go spends 8 minutes extracting Go on Windows CI

shipmates CI runs on my own ephemerd runners. On Windows those jobs run inside a Hyper-V utility VM. The windows-x64 leg kept timing out in actions/setup-go. Here’s the log from PR #48:

20:58:46  Setup go version spec 1.26.6
20:58:46  Attempting to download 1.26.6...     <- tool-cache MISS
20:58:48  Acquiring 1.26.6 from ...zip
20:58:53  Extracting Go...
21:06:46  ERROR: The action 'Run actions/setup-go@v5' has timed out after 8 minutes

Seven seconds from the start of the step to Extracting Go.... Then almost eight minutes extracting until the step timeout killed it.

item.title: Kata Containers for CI: Boot Cost Isn't the Problem, File I/O Is
item.description: Of the three platforms ephemerd runs jobs on, Linux has the weakest isolation. Windows jobs get a Hyper-V isolated container with its own kernel. macOS jobs get a whole VM. A Linux job is an ordinary runc container sharing the host kernel. A kernel escape from a Linux job is a host compromise. Kata Containers fixes that by putting each container in a lightweight VM with its own kernel. It plugs into containerd as just another runtime handler. So I added it in #155, measured it, and left it off by default. This post is why.
